title: Tibet's first king
hookLine: Songtsen Gampo and his two Buddhist queens, from Nepal and China

lines: A PRINCESS FROM NEPAL, ONE FROM CHINA.
cards: High on the plateau, a king is building an empire. Songtsen Gampo, the Tibetan histories say, ruled Tibet and pushed its borders outward. He made alliances by marriage, taking wives from powerful neighbors.
Two of them came over the mountains: a princess from Nepal and a princess from China. Each one, the story goes, brought something with her that would outlast the empire. Not gold.
Not soldiers. An image of the Buddha.

teach.b: Tibetan histories give the queens names. From Nepal came Bhrikuti. From China came Wencheng.
Each, tradition says, carried a sacred image of the Buddha, and temples were raised in Lhasa to house them.
One of those images, the statue called the Jowo, is linked by tradition to Wencheng, and it is honored in the Jokhang temple in Lhasa today.
Pilgrims walk around the temple and stretch out full length on the stones in front of it. The same histories credit the king's reign with another gift.
A minister, tradition says, was sent to India and came back with a way to write Tibetan, so that one day the teachings could be translated.

Later Tibetans remember Songtsen Gampo as the first of the dharma kings, the kings who welcomed the teaching, and they tell his story in sacred terms: the king as a form of Chenrezig, the bodhisattva of compassion, and the two queens as forms of Tara.
Historians read these accounts carefully. They come from later Tibetan histories, and how much the king practiced himself is debated. But notice what the story chooses to remember.
The arrivals. Two women who left home, crossed the mountains, and carried something precious into a land that didn't yet have it. The teaching came in quietly, as a gift in a bride's baggage.

how: Tibetan Buddhists visit the Jokhang in Lhasa to honor the Jowo statue, walking around the temple and making full-length prostrations, and they remember Songtsen Gampo and his queens in histories and festivals.

games.q: you're a princess sent across the mountains to marry a foreign king. you may bring one precious thing. what do you bring?
games.why: tradition says each queen brought an image of the Buddha. the Jowo, linked to Wencheng, is honored in Lhasa today.

practice: Bring to mind a person who carried something good into your life from somewhere else, a recipe, a song, a way of praying, a way of being kind, and picture the road they traveled to reach you.
If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if not, simply hold their face in mind with gratitude.
